body:
Meaning of heritage conservation

Cultural heritage consists of places, objects, knowledge and traditions inherited from earlier generations that are valued for their historical, artistic, archaeological, scientific or social significance. Heritage conservation means identifying these values, preventing unnecessary loss and ensuring that important evidence and cultural practices can be passed to future generations.

An old structure may provide several kinds of evidence at once. Its stones reveal construction methods, inscriptions preserve historical information, and its location may explain the development of a settlement. Conservation therefore protects more than the visible appearance of a monument. It also protects the features and surroundings that make the monument meaningful.

Heritage conservation is the planned protection, care and management of culturally or historically significant heritage so that its important values survive for future generations.

Major forms of heritage

Tangible cultural heritage

Tangible heritage has a physical form. Immovable examples include forts, temples, stepwells, archaeological sites, historic buildings and groups of buildings. Movable examples include sculptures, coins, manuscripts, paintings and archaeological objects that can be transported.

Intangible cultural heritage

Intangible heritage consists of living practices, expressions, knowledge and skills that communities recognise as part of their heritage. Oral traditions, festivals and traditional craftsmanship are examples. Although a craftsperson may produce a physical object, the inherited knowledge required to make it is intangible heritage.

Natural heritage

Natural heritage includes significant natural features, habitats and landscapes. The UNESCO World Heritage framework recognises both cultural and natural heritage, including properties that satisfy the requirements of both categories.

Conservation is not the same as restoration

  • Conservation: the broad process of protecting heritage significance through research, maintenance, suitable interventions and continued management.
  • Preservation: keeping existing historic material and features safe from deterioration or unnecessary alteration.
  • Restoration: returning a structure or feature towards an earlier condition that can be established through reliable evidence. Restoration should not depend on guesswork.
  • Reconstruction: rebuilding a lost or substantially destroyed element. Because it introduces new material, reconstruction requires particular care and clear justification.
  • Adaptive reuse: giving a historic building a compatible present-day function while retaining the features that express its significance.

These approaches are not interchangeable. A damaged wall may need stabilisation rather than complete rebuilding. A historic house may remain useful as a residence, while another building may be adapted for a museum if the changes do not destroy important features.

A Gujarat example: Rani-ki-Vav

Rani-ki-Vav at Patan is an 11th-century stepwell recognised for its elaborate sculptural decoration and subterranean water architecture. The structure no longer functions as a working water well, but that does not remove its historical or architectural importance. Conservation protects its surviving stonework, spatial arrangement and setting rather than attempting to make every part appear newly constructed.

The example demonstrates a central principle: the value of heritage does not depend only on whether it still performs its original function.

Prelims focus

  • Tangible heritage has a physical form; intangible heritage includes living knowledge, practices and skills.
  • Immovable heritage includes monuments and archaeological sites; movable heritage includes manuscripts and sculptures.
  • Conservation is broader than restoration or reconstruction.
  • Rani-ki-Vav is located at Patan in Gujarat.
  • Trap: A monument does not lose its heritage value merely because its original function has ended.

[Sources: UNESCO, Convention concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage, 1972, Articles 1–2, accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003, Article 2, accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen’s Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat,” Brief Synthesis and Integrity sections, accessed 23 November 2026; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Chapter 1, “Crafts Heritage,” printed pp. 9–14.]

pictures.alt: Conservation workers examine stone carvings at Rani-ki-Vav while visitors observe its descending steps and pillared sandstone architecture from a distance.
pictures.caption: Conservation protects historic structures while allowing people to understand and experience them.

title: Understanding Heritage Conservation: What Is Protected and Why

body:
Why several authorities are involved

India has monuments and heritage places of national, state and local importance. Their protection involves different laws and institutions. The authority responsible for a site depends on its legal designation, ownership and location. A UNESCO inscription may add international conservation responsibilities, but it does not replace Indian law or transfer ownership to UNESCO.

Archaeological Survey of India

The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) was established in 1861 and functions under the Ministry of Culture, Government of India. Alexander Cunningham played a foundational role in its establishment and became its first Director-General.

The ASI investigates and documents archaeological remains, undertakes archaeological excavations, studies inscriptions, and conserves monuments and archaeological sites declared to be of national importance. Its field organisation includes archaeological circles responsible for conservation and related work in their jurisdictions.

A centrally protected monument is a monument protected under the relevant central legislation because of its national importance. The ASI does not automatically control every old building in India.

National Monuments Authority

The National Monuments Authority (NMA) was established under the amendments made in 2010 to the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains legislation. It has an important role in assessing the heritage implications of proposed construction and other works around centrally protected monuments.

The NMA makes recommendations under the statutory permission system. The designated Competent Authority issues the applicable permission or no-objection certificate in accordance with the law. The NMA and ASI have related but different responsibilities: the ASI is principally concerned with archaeological protection and conservation, while the NMA has a defined role in regulating works near centrally protected sites.

Heritage protection by the Government of Gujarat

The Gujarat Directorate of Archaeology and Museums is a state-level institution concerned with archaeological and museum heritage. The state archaeological organisation dates from 1964. Gujarat also has the Gujarat Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1965, which provides for protection of monuments and archaeological remains other than those declared to be of national importance.

This creates an important distinction: a monument may be protected by the Union government or under state law. A site does not become centrally protected merely because it is located in Gujarat or is historically significant.

Role of local bodies, owners and communities

Municipal bodies influence heritage conservation through land-use planning, building permissions, infrastructure and the protection of historic neighbourhoods. Owners, religious trusts and local residents may also be directly responsible for the care and continued use of heritage buildings.

At places such as Champaner-Pavagadh, different public departments, religious trusts and other stakeholders must cooperate because the protected landscape contains archaeological remains, living places of worship and land under different forms of management.

Constitutional provisions

ProvisionNatureCore responsibility
Article 49Directive Principle of State PolicyThe State must protect monuments, places and objects of artistic or historic interest declared by or under a law made by Parliament to be of national importance from damage, destruction, removal and related threats.
Article 51A(f)Fundamental DutyEvery citizen has a duty to value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture.

Article 49 is directed to the State, whereas Article 51A(f) concerns citizens. Neither provision, by itself, constitutes a notification declaring a particular monument centrally protected. Such legal protection is established through the applicable legislation and procedures.

Prelims focus

  • ASI was established in 1861 and functions under the Ministry of Culture.
  • Alexander Cunningham was the first Director-General of the ASI.
  • NMA was established under the 2010 amendments to the central monuments law.
  • Gujarat's principal state monuments legislation dates from 1965.
  • Article 49 concerns the State; Article 51A(f) states a Fundamental Duty of citizens.
  • Trap: ASI protection, state protection and UNESCO inscription are different legal or institutional arrangements.

[Sources: Ministry of Culture, Government of India, “Archaeological Survey of India” and “Archaeology,” accessed 23 November 2026; National Monuments Authority, Frequently Asked Questions, accessed 23 November 2026; Gujarat Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1965, Preamble and preliminary provisions; NITI Aayog, Gujarat Directorate of Archaeology and Museums institutional information, accessed 23 November 2026; Constitution of India, Articles 49 and 51A(f), Legislative Department text, accessed 23 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, “Bricks, Beads and Bones,” printed p. 6.]

pictures.alt: ASI and NMA have distinct Union roles, Gujarat handles state heritage, local bodies support planning and care, and UNESCO recognises and monitors without owning sites.
pictures.caption: Heritage protection involves several authorities whose responsibilities depend on the site's legal status.

title: Heritage Institutions in India: ASI, Gujarat Authorities and Constitutional Duties

body:
The central monuments law of 1958

The principal central law is the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, usually called the AMASR Act. It provides for the preservation of ancient and historical monuments and archaeological sites and remains declared to be of national importance.

Under its definition, an ancient monument generally refers to a structure, erection or monument of historical, archaeological or artistic interest that has existed for not less than 100 years. The law also covers specified remains and associated elements. Archaeological sites and remains have a related statutory definition.

However, meeting the age requirement does not automatically make a structure a centrally protected monument. The declaration of national importance must follow the relevant legal provisions: Section 3 recognises earlier statutory declarations, while Section 4 provides for a new declaration by Central Government notification after 2 months' notice of its intention and consideration of objections.

100 years is an age condition in the statutory definition, not an automatic certificate of central protection. A 150-year-old house may be historically valuable without being declared a monument of national importance.

Prohibited and regulated areas around centrally protected monuments

The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2010 strengthened controls on activities around centrally protected monuments and sites.

The standard statutory arrangement is based on the protected monument's or site's notified limits:

  • Prohibited area: the first 100 metres beyond the limits of the centrally protected monument or site.
  • Regulated area: the next 200 metres, measured outward from the limit of the prohibited area.

Thus, the standard regulated belt lies approximately 100 to 300 metres from the protected boundary. The Central Government may extend either belt by notification in the Official Gazette, having regard to the monument's or site's classification; extending the prohibited area also requires the NMA's recommendation. Measurements are taken from the protected limits, not necessarily from the visual centre of a monument.

What construction is permitted?

New construction and reconstruction are generally prohibited in the prohibited area; construction by an archaeological officer is excepted, and drainage, public sanitation, public water-supply and electricity works are excluded from the statutory definition of construction. Repairs or renovation of structures existing before 16 June 1992 or subsequently built with the Director-General's approval require prior permission from the Competent Authority and should not be confused with permission for a new building.

In the regulated area, construction, reconstruction, repair or renovation require prior permission. The proposal is examined through the designated Competent Authority, with the NMA performing its statutory recommendation role. A municipal building approval alone does not replace a permission required under the AMASR framework.

These restrictions apply to centrally protected monuments and sites. They must not be assumed to apply automatically to every state-protected building or every property recognised by UNESCO.

Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972

The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972 concerns the control of export, trade and specified registration requirements relating to antiquities and art treasures. It addresses a different problem from building restrictions around protected monuments.

Category or lawKey age or focusMain distinction
Ancient monument under the AMASR ActAt least 100 yearsHistorical, archaeological or artistic structure; national protection requires proper declaration.
Antiquity under the 1972 ActGenerally at least 100 yearsSpecified objects and works of archaeological or historical interest.
Manuscript, record or document under the 1972 ActAt least 75 yearsA separate age threshold applies within the statutory antiquities definition.
Gujarat monuments law, 1965State-level protectionAddresses qualifying monuments and remains other than those declared nationally important.

A manuscript and a historic fort are both forms of tangible heritage, but the legal provisions dealing with movable antiquities and protected immovable monuments are not identical.

Applying the distinctions

If a proposed building is situated 150 metres beyond the notified limit of a centrally protected monument, it normally falls in the regulated area, not the prohibited area. Whether the work may proceed depends on the applicable permission requirements; its location inside the regulated belt does not mean that every proposal is automatically approved.

Prelims focus

  • AMASR Act: 1958; important amendments: 2010.
  • Standard prohibited area: first 100 metres beyond the centrally protected monument's boundary.
  • Standard regulated area: next 200 metres, extending approximately to 300 metres from that boundary.
  • Antiquities and Art Treasures Act: 1972.
  • Under the 1972 Act, the general 100-year threshold differs from the 75-year threshold for manuscripts, records and documents.
  • Trap: A building's age alone does not establish its status as a centrally protected monument.

[Sources: Archaeological Survey of India, Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, Sections 2–4 and provisions on protected areas; Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2010, provisions introducing Sections 20A–20C and the permission framework; National Monuments Authority, Frequently Asked Questions, especially prohibited and regulated areas and permissions, accessed 23 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972, Section 2; Gujarat Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1965, Preamble.]

pictures.alt: From the notified protected boundary, the prohibited belt extends 100 metres and the next regulated belt extends 200 metres, to approximately 300 metres.
pictures.caption: The 100-metre prohibited area and the next 200-metre regulated area are separate legal zones.

title: Indian Monuments Laws: Protected Sites, Antiquities and Construction Restrictions
